To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the soluble mediators, lymphokines, released from stimulated lymphoid cells activate immunosuppressive monocytes.
the supernatants (SUPs) of phytohae-magglutinin‐stimulated human lymphocytes contain factors that can activate monocytes to become immunosup-pressive.
the supernatants from activated lymphocytes can activate immunosuppressive monocytes, which can in turn suppress the proliferative responses of autologous lymphoid cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunoregulatory role of soluble mediators released by stimulated lymphocytes and their effects on the immunological responses.
the immunological role of monocytes‐macro‐phages and their interaction with other lymphoid cell populations.
the study of immunological phenomena in vitro, and in particular with the role of monocytes‐ macrophages in lymphoid cell activation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PHA‐stimuIated lymphoid cells release a soluble factor which activates monocytes‐macrphages to become immunosuppresive.
the lymphoid cells, when stimulated by PHA, produce a factor that activates the monocytes to produce immunosuppression, and that the immunosuppression is mediated through the monocytes.
the results presented here show that lymphokine preparations can activate monocytes in such a way as to make them suppressive for lymphocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lymphokines released during the PHA‐stimulation of human lymphoid cells can induce the production of immunosuppressive monocytes‐macraphages.
the immunosuppressive effect of lymphokines on T cells is due to the activation of monocytes‐ macrophages.
lymphokines can be immunosuppressive by activating monocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunosuppressive activity of lymphokines is not restricted to the T cell system, but can be exerted through monocytes‐macrrophages.
lymphokines may play a role in the immunosuppression associated with chronic infections and cancer, as well as in autoimmune disease.
monocyte‐macrophages may be involved in the immunosuppression induced by lymphokines.
